meta.title: Buying Absolution
meta.logline: Is DEI a modern indulgence? Chapter 6 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on opportunity versus outcome, diversity statements, dropped tests, hiring in medicine and safety, and brand backlash, with the strongest counterpoints.
meta.source: Chapter 6 ('Selling Indulgences') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: university test-policy announcements (2024); FAA litigation; AB InBev results (2023).
meta.disclaimer: Original animation, characters, voice and music. An homage to flat-design science explainers. Not affiliated with any channel, author or publisher.

els.text: an indulgence

As soon as a coin in the coffer rings,
a soul from purgatory springs.
Martin Luther, 1517: forgiveness can’t be bought

lines.text: Five hundred years ago, if you were worried about your sins, the Church offered a solution. You could buy an indulgence, a certificate said to shorten your punishment after death.
A slogan of the time went: as soon as a coin in the coffer rings, a soul from purgatory springs.
In 1517, a monk named Martin Luther objected. Forgiveness, he argued, could not be bought.

els.text: Saad spells it DIE, on purpose

lines.text: In chapter six of Suicidal Empathy, Gad Saad argues that modern institutions have revived the trade. The sin is privilege, and the indulgence is diversity, equity and inclusion.
He rearranges the letters to spell DIE, and he means it as a provocation.

els.text: equality of opportunity: same rules
equality of outcome: same finish
different starting lines?

lines.text: Saad's argument starts with a distinction. Equality of opportunity means everyone runs the race under the same rules.
Equality of outcome means everyone should finish together. In 2020, Kamala Harris shared a video describing equity as treatment where everyone ends up in the same place.
Saad argues that because people differ in talents, interests and choices, equal outcomes can only be produced by treating people unequally.
Supporters reply that people don't all start from the same line either, and a little help at the start is simply fairness.

els.title: Job ads asking for a diversity statement (studies Saad cites)

lines.text: Much of his evidence comes from universities. One analysis he cites found that about one in five American faculty job ads asked applicants for a diversity statement.
In a Canadian sample, nearly all of them did: four hundred and seventy-seven out of four hundred and eighty-nine.

els.text: the bill: students and taxpayers

lines.text: Some Canadian research chairs were restricted to candidates from particular groups, and the University of Michigan was reported to employ hundreds of DEI staff, at a cost of tens of millions of dollars a year.
Saad calls these indulgences: institutions pay to feel absolved, and students and taxpayers pick up the bill.

els.text: tests dropped "for fairness"
brought them back: tests help find poor, talented students

lines.text: Many universities also dropped standardized tests, in the name of fairness.
Interestingly, several, including MIT, Dartmouth and Yale, later brought them back, saying test scores actually helped them find talented students from poor backgrounds.

els.text: Saad: skill first

lines.text: Saad is most alarmed when this reaches medicine and safety.

He points to a proposed update of Canada's framework for training doctors, which he says puts values like anti-oppression ahead of medical expertise, and to a 2022 University of Minnesota medical school oath that pledged to honour Indigenous ways of healing and to fight white supremacy.

els.text: FAA hiring questionnaire, 2014
screened out many top aviation graduates · lawsuits followed
Los Angeles fires, January 2025

He got himself in the wrong place
if I have to carry him out of a fire.

lines.text: He cites air traffic controller hiring at the US Federal Aviation Administration, which in 2014 introduced a questionnaire that screened out many top graduates of aviation programs. The agency was later sued over it.

And during the Los Angeles fires of January 2025, earlier remarks by a deputy fire chief went viral. Asked whether she could carry a man out of a fire, she had said he got himself in the wrong place if she had to carry him out.
Saad's point is simple: when lives are at stake, skill has to come first.

els.text: boycott: lost its #1 US spot
a rebrand ad with no cars
sell products, not virtue?

lines.text: Then there's woke capitalism. In 2023, Bud Light sent a personalised can to a transgender influencer. A boycott followed, and sales fell so far that it lost its place as America's best-selling beer.
In 2024, Jaguar unveiled a rebrand with a bright, stylish ad that showed no cars at all. It was widely mocked.
Saad's verdict: when companies sell virtue instead of products, customers notice.

els.text: identical CVs, different names: callback gaps persist
wider outreach doesn’t lower the bar
some programs badly designed, and supporters say so
open the doors wide, then pick the best

lines.text: Critics have answers.
Discrimination hasn't vanished. Studies that send out identical CVs under different names still find gaps in who gets called back.
Outreach that widens the pool of applicants doesn't lower the bar. And the research on diverse teams, while mixed, isn't nothing.
Many companies are simply responding to customers. And some DEI programs really were badly designed, which plenty of their own supporters admit.
Shared ground: open the doors as wide as you can, then pick the best person who walks through them.

els.text: you can’t buy your way to goodness

lines.text: Luther's objection was that you can't buy your way to goodness. Saad's is that you can't train, hire, or market your way there either.
